                                                          Abstract
      We develop a new approach for clustering non-spherical (i.e., arbitrary component covariances)
      Gaussian mixture models via a subroutine based on the sum-of-squares method that finds a low-
      dimensional separation-preserving projection of the input data. Our method provides a non-spherical
      analog of the classical dimension reduction based on singular value decomposition that, among sev-
      eral other applications, forms a key component of the celebrated spherical clustering algorithm of
      Vempala and Wang (Vempala and Wang, 2004).

1. Introduction
In this work, we revisit the problem of clustering a high-dimensional Gaussian mixture model.
Specifically, we are interested in algorithms
                                     P        that take i.i.d. samples drawn from a mixture of k d-
dimensional Gaussian distributions i≤k wi N (µi , Σi ) as input, where k ≪ d. The goal is to output
a good clustering of the data: partitioning the points based on the component that generated them,
with at most 1% misclassified points. Such a goal is statistically possible only if the component
Gaussians are pairwise well-separated, i.e., have a total variation distance of at least 1 − O(wmin )
(or “overlap” ≪ wmin ) between them.1

The Gaussian mixture model (GMM) has a history beginning more than a century ago in the work of
Pearson Pearson (1894). In the last 50 years, the model has been extensively utilized in applications
in science and engineering. Starting with Dasgupta (1999), it has become a central model studied
in algorithmic statistics. And, recently, an exciting line of work has even found deep connections
between the hardness of clustering non-spherical Gaussian mixture models and lattice problems
pivotal to modern cryptography Bruna et al. (2021); Gupte et al. (2022). From an algorithm design
perspective, the problem of learning GMMs has long served as a benchmark for provable tech-
niques in algorithmic statistics. Indeed, advances for the problem over the years are closely linked
to the development of new broadly applicable tools in statistical learning, such as dimension reduc-
tion Vempala and Wang (2004); Belkin and Sinha (2010), the random projection method Kalai et al.
(2010); Moitra and Valiant (2010), the method of moments Kalai et al. (2010); Moitra and Valiant
(2010), tensor methods Hsu and Kakade (2013); Ge et al. (2015), outlier-filters Diakonikolas et al.
(2018), and the sum-of-squares method Kothari and Steinhardt (2017); Hopkins and Li (2018b);
Diakonikolas et al. (2020); Bakshi and Kothari (2020).

In his pioneering work, Dasgupta Dasgupta (1999) began the quest for provably efficient algo-
rithms for Gaussian mixture models by focusing on the case of clustering spherical (i.e., when all
Σi s are scalings of Id ) mixtures. This quest Sanjeev and Kannan (2001); Achlioptas and McSh-
erry (2005) culminated in algorithms to cluster mixtures with a dimension-independent pairwise
component separation Vempala and Wang (2004). Their work relied on a separation-preserving
projection to a low-dimensional subspace based on singular value decomposition. The quantitative
separation requirement was substantially improved to near-optimal in recent years Diakonikolas
et al. (2018); Kothari and Steinhardt (2017); Hopkins and Li (2018b); Liu and Li (2022), and the
resulting algorithms also have outlier-robust analogs that tolerate a constant fraction of arbitrary
outliers Diakonikolas et al. (2019); Lai et al. (2016).

The non-spherical case (i.e., arbitrary Σi s) has proved more challenging. The first clustering al-
gorithm for such mixtures formed a crucial subroutine in the celebrated works Belkin and Sinha
(2010); Moitra and Valiant (2010) that gave the first polynomial-time algorithms for learning an
arbitrary (potentially non-clusterable) GMM. Their work required running time and sample com-

A sub-exponential algorithm for GMMs? At first glance, this might seem like the final word on
the problem — we have algorithms with a cost that aligns perfectly with the lower bounds in various
models. But a deeper dive suggests fascinating twists hiding just beneath the surface.
The hardness results above are based on the parallel pancakes construction that starts with a 1-
dimensional mixture of k Gaussians which matches the standard Gaussian distribution in its first
Ω(k) moments Diakonikolas et al. (2017). The “hard” mixture is then obtained by planting the
1-D construction in a random direction (with all orthogonal directions being standard Gaussian in
all components). Importantly, the resulting hard family of mixture models has (1) components of
exponentially small weight, i.e., wmin ∼ 2−k , and (2) non-zero means.
What happens if we restrict ourselves to mixture models where the minimum mixing weight, wmin ,
is at least 1/poly(k)? Or if all the components are centered? These are natural and well-studied
settings in their own right, capturing problems such as mixtures of linear regressions and sub-
space clustering (covariances with distinct range spaces) Chen et al. (2020); Diakonikolas and Kane
(2020).
Known algorithmic techniques do not appear to have the power to exploit such natural structures
of the mixture components. Indeed, the clustering algorithms in Bakshi and Kothari (2020); Di-
akonikolas et al. (2020) need dpoly(k) time and samples even for equiweighted (i.e., wmin = 1/k)
mixtures with centered components.2 Technically, this is because the total variation separation be-

Our results In this paper, we present a natural non-spherical analog of the influential dimen-
sion reduction technique of Vempala and Wang (2004), which gave the first algorithm for clus-
tering spherical mixtures with dimension-independent separation requirements. Specifically, we
show an efficient algorithm based on a new sum-of-squares SDP relaxation that identifies a low-
dimensional projection of the input mixture, preserving the total variation separation between at
least one pair of initial components. Unlike the method in Buhai and Steurer (2023), identifying
this low-dimensional subspace allows us to partially cluster (i.e., find a cluster-preserving partition
of the data) and iterate while accumulating only a small error.
As applications, we obtain new algorithms for outlier-robust clustering of well-separated5 centered
Gaussian mixtures and mixtures with the same (albeit unknown and non-spherical) covariances.

A.4. Partial Clustering Definitions
In this section we introduce some definitions and notation relating to clustering that we use in our
analysis.
Definition 31 (Containment) For a collection of samples T coming from a mixture of components
and for a subset S ⊆ T , a component i is contained in S if a (1 − wmin )-fraction of the samples in
T from component i are in S. Let comp(S) denote the indices of components contained in S.
Definition 32 (Corruptions) For a collection of samples T coming from a mixture of components
and for a subset S ⊆ T , let corr(S) denote the number of corrupted samples in S, defined as the
number of samples in S that do not belong to a component in comp(S) plus the number of samples
in T \ S that belong to a component in comp(S).
Definition 33 (ε-good partial clustering) For a collection of samples T coming from a mixture of
components, we call a set S = {S1 , . . . , Sk′ } with S1 , . . . , Sk′ ⊆ T a partial clustering of the
samples if S1 , ..., Sk′ are disjoint, S1 ∪ . . . ∪ Sk′ = T , and comp(S1 ), . . . , comp(Sk′ ) > 0. We say
that a partial clustering S is (1 − ε)-good if all S ∈ S have corr(S)/|S| ≤ ε.
Definition 34 (Refinement of a partial clustering) For a collection of samples T coming from a
mixture of components, given two partial clusterings of the samples S, S ′ , we say that S ′ is a
refinement of S if for all S ′ ∈ S ′ there exists some S ∈ S such that S ′ ⊆ S and if |S ′ | > |S|.
